title: Names in pairs
hook: the First and Last, the Manifest and Hidden, the Withholder and Expander
tomorrow: an old man with no children asks for an heir. which Name?

segments.voice: Yesterday, your name for Him: Dadi's Ya Latif, Jordan's grandmother's Father, and an honest difference between them. The line: my name for him. This whole week ran from the Originator to the Most Patient, and today they come back.
screen: `MY NAME FOR HIM.` → `THE WEEK COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: At noon the stars are all still up there. Daylight doesn't erase them; it hides them. Something can be completely present and completely out of sight at once. Dadi's first night in the new room, Amira finds her by the window, eyes wet, smiling. "Sad or happy?" Amira asks. Dadi says: "Both, beta. Why does it have to be one?" The Qur'an has been saying that about Allah all along.
screen: `STARS AT NOON.` → `SAD OR HAPPY?` → `BOTH. WHY ONE?`

segments.voice: Surah al-Hadid, in Pickthall's words: "He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward; and He is Knower of all things." Not first and then later last. Both, at once. In a du'a from Sahih Muslim, the Prophet, peace be upon him, unfolds it: You are the First, nothing before You; the Last, nothing after You; the Outward, nothing above You; the Inward, nothing beneath You. Other Names travel in pairs too. Surah al-Baqarah: "Allah straiteneth and enlargeth." The Withholder and the Expander, Al-Qabid and Al-Basit. Scholars of the Names advise saying such pairs together, so that neither half becomes the whole picture. A lean month isn't a verdict; a good month isn't a prize. The same hand holds both. And this week's Names were already doing it. The Originator who begins, the Inheritor to whom it all returns. The Everlasting who stays, the Patient who waits. Here's the thing to tell a friend: in Islam some Names are meant to be said as a pair, the way Dadi answered.
screen: `THE FIRST AND THE LAST, AT ONCE.` · `OUTWARD AND INWARD.` · `HE STRAITENETH AND ENLARGETH.` · `SAY THE PAIR, NOT THE HALF.` · then, large: `HE HOLDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and hold one pair for the whole sit. On the in-breath, the First; on the out-breath, the Last. When the mind tries to pick one, let both be true at once, without choosing between them.
Names in pairs: the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, said together so neither half stands alone.
For the week's end: he holds both, the lean month and the full one, the sad and the glad. A week of names, gathered.

screen: `DAY 1575 COUNTS.` → `THE NAMES, GATHERED · 2 OF 3 · YEAR FIVE, 149 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: AN OLD MAN WITH NO CHILDREN ASKS FOR AN HEIR. WHICH NAME?`

howItsDone: Muslims often say paired Names together in remembrance, al-Qabid with al-Basit, ad-Darr with an-Nafi', and recite 57:3 among the Names of the First and the Last.

match.prompt: the week's Names — tap the pairs.

myth: the Inward means Allah is absent or far away
He is the Outward and the Inward at once: present and unseen, like stars at noon.
Surah al-Hadid calls Him the First and the Last
"He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward."

fork.setup: your uncle's shop had a great month, then a dead one. he asks you, half joking, if God is mad at him now. what do the paired Names say?
options: the same hand withholds and expands; a lean month isn't a verdict.
a good month means He's pleased, and a dead month means He's angry.
money isn't in Allah's hands at all; it's just how the market goes.
fork.reveal: "Allah straiteneth and enlargeth." the pair is said together so neither half, the lean or the full, gets read as the whole picture.

original.note: Arabic: the First and the Last, the opening pair of 57:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: God starts things first and finishes them last, in order.
what it means: He is First and Last, Outward and Inward, at once; pairs keep either half from becoming the whole.
what a scholar hears: 57:3 unfolded in the du'a of Sahih Muslim 2713; 2:245 for al-Qabid and al-Basit.
guess: Names said together so neither half stands alone
two Names that cancel each other out in a du'a
a Name repeated twice to make it stronger

chat.says: dadi's first night here. she said she's sad AND happy. is that even possible
options: Very possible. Even His Names come in pairs, said together. She can hold both.
Not really. One feeling always wins out; she's probably mostly happy.
Tell her to choose grateful. Sad means she isn't trusting Allah enough.
chat.meaning: He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, at once. Pairs are said together; Dadi's 'both' fits.
